questions.prompt: A pupil is rebuilding a paragraph about living in the city centre. The sentence just before reads: "It also saves you an hour of travelling every single day." The next sentence has to bring in a drawback. Which of these opens it?

options.text: On the other hand,
This is especially
To begin with,
What is more,

questions.explanation: The paragraph has been on the side of the advantages and now has to change sides, and the phrase that turns to the opposite side is "On the other hand,". "What is more," adds a second point to the side you are already on, so it would promise the reader another advantage and hand him a drawback instead — the commonest fault in a rebuilt paragraph. "This is especially" develops the sentence in front of it rather than turning anywhere, and it cannot even stand on its own: This has to point back at something. "To begin with," opens a list, and nothing is being opened here — two sentences have already gone by.

questions.prompt: A hotel brochure calls one of its buildings a leisure club. What does the word leisure tell you about it?

options.text: It amuses you rather than trains you.
It is for the hours that belong to you.
It is free of charge.
It is reserved for members of the hotel.

questions.explanation: leisure names a stretch of time — the hours you are free to use as you please — so a leisure club is the club you use in those hours: "It is for the hours that belong to you." "It amuses you rather than trains you." reads leisure as a kind of amusement, which is why the same guess puts the gym on the wrong side of the word: a gym trains you and still stands in the leisure club. "It is free of charge." confuses free time with a free price. "It is reserved for members of the hotel." answers the word club instead of the word leisure, and a hotel's leisure club is open to every guest in the building.

questions.prompt: The verb relax carries its beat on the second syllable: re-LAX. You are now reading the module's words aloud and marking the beat in each one. Where does it fall in relaxing?

options.text: at the beginning, on re-
evenly, with no syllable louder
on -ing, at the very end
on -lax-, in the middle

questions.explanation: The ending -ing adds a syllable and leaves the stress exactly where the base word already had it, so re-LAX becomes re-LAX-ing: the beat stays "on -lax-, in the middle". "at the beginning, on re-" applies a rule that does not exist — English does not pull the beat to the front when a word grows. "on -ing, at the very end" moves it onto the new syllable, which is what -tion and -sion do (EDucate becomes eduCAtion) but never what -ing does. "evenly, with no syllable louder" describes no English word of more than one syllable: one syllable always carries the beat.

questions.prompt: A pupil is putting the marks back into this bare line: "the box held the tools we needed pliers a torch two spanners and a roll of tape". Which version is right?

options.text: The box held the tools we needed, pliers, a torch, two spanners and a roll of tape.
The box held the tools we needed. Pliers, a torch, two spanners and a roll of tape.
The box held the tools we needed: pliers, a torch, two spanners and a roll of tape.
The box held the tools we needed; pliers, a torch, two spanners and a roll of tape.

questions.explanation: A general term about to be opened out into its members takes a colon, and here the members are the four tools: "The box held the tools we needed: pliers, a torch, two spanners and a roll of tape." The version with a comma after needed turns the tools we needed into a fifth item standing beside the pliers and the torch, so the box ends up holding five things instead of four. The version with a full stop leaves Pliers, a torch, two spanners and a roll of tape with no verb at all, which is a list and not a sentence. The version with a semicolon uses the mark that joins two complete sentences, and the second half here is not one.

questions.prompt: A pupil is rebuilding a paragraph and finds this sentence among the pieces: "Such an evening leaves the whole family too tired to talk." What does the word Such tell her about where the sentence can stand?

options.text: It can stand anywhere, because such is only an intensifier.
It cannot come first, because the evening has to be described before it.
It must come first, because a word like such announces the whole subject.
It must come last, because such always closes a paragraph.

questions.explanation: Such points backwards, exactly as This and That do: it means an evening of the kind just described, so some earlier sentence has to have described one. That places the piece after that sentence and rules out the first square — "It cannot come first, because the evening has to be described before it." "It must come first, because a word like such announces the whole subject." reads a backward-pointing word as an opening one, which is the trap. "It can stand anywhere, because such is only an intensifier." confuses this such with the such of such a long day, where it does only intensify. "It must come last, because such always closes a paragraph." invents a rule: a backward-pointing sentence can be followed by three more.
